Intel and Advanced Micro Devices dropped 4% each and Marvell Technology retreated almost 6%. Energy stocks — Several energy producers gained in the wake of higher prices for West Texas Intermediate and Brent crude oil as tensions in the Middle East simmered. APA advanced 2% while EOG Resources added 1.6%. Cybersecurity stocks — The group saw strong gains as worries around AI safety increased following warnings from industry leaders Dario Amodei and Sam Altman that the technology may be developing too quickly. First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR) added 6%, Amplify Cybersecurity ETF (HACK) climbed more than 7% and Global X Cybersecurity ETF (BUG) soared 10%. Cybersecurity providers Palo Alto Networks jumped 13% and Zscaler and CrowdStrike both soared 15%. AI infrastructure stocks — Shares of Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell almost 9% following growing concerns about AI development and safety. Evercore ISI downgraded HPE to inline from outperform. IT solutions provider Super Micro Computer fell 6%. Affirm — Shares added more than 3% following a Wolfe Research upgrade to outperform. The researcher said there's a buying opportunity after Affirm's recent post-earnings decline. Baldwin Insurance Group – The insurance distribution company jumped almost 8% after agreeing to go private. An entity formed by Sequence Holdings and DFO Management will buy Baldwin in an all-cash transaction valued at $32.50 a share, or $7.7 billion. Elmet Group – The maker of precision-engineered parts soared 36%. The Department of War announced a $450 million investment in the company, aiming to strengthen the nation's tungsten supply chain. Elmet plans to use more than $165 million of the proceeds to expand critical infrastructure facilities in Maine, Michigan and Ohio. Roblox – The gaming platform jumped more than 11% after announcing new capabilities at its developers conference . The advancements aim to make the game more accessible and enhance the experience for creators, including adding AI-powered tools. — CNBC's Darla Mercado, Toby Burns, Ananya Chetia, Fred Imbert and Nick Wells contributed reporting.

Microsoft sets limits for future AI models as industry throttles frontier development
headlines.summary: Microsoft wants to be seen as a responsible AI entity as it ramps up model development alongside partners Anthropic and OpenAI.
headlines.article_text: Microsoft sets AI model limits as industry throttles development Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Microsoft issued a provisional code of conduct that sets limits on its future artificial intelligence models. The company will listen to outside input before rolling out an update. The release comes as AI figureheads propose slowing the pace of AI evolution after one researcher said frontier labs are "gambling with our lives." In this article MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, speaks at an event commemorating the 50th anniversary of the company at Microsoft headquarters in Redmond, Washington, on April 4, 2025. David Ryder | Bloomberg | Getty Images Microsoft has posted a provisional code of conduct that would impose restrictions on its artificial intelligence models, days after Anthropic and OpenAI leaders agreed to slow development speed. The company behind Windows and Office products hopes to be seen as a responsible actor in AI, where it's a prominent cloud supplier. "We got feedback from people that they wanted to see even more explicit commitment to AI always working in service of people and not trying to replace them," Mustafa Suleyman, who heads up the company's model development , told CNBC in an interview. "We saw a lot of feedback around AI not creating dependence, not being sycophantic, that it was always there to kind of promote human judgment and human autonomy and agency." Microsoft chose to put out the guidelines now given the recent discourse, although they've been in the works for about five months, said Suleyman. AI practitioners and members of the public have become more vocal about their worries as the technology becomes increasingly capable. Last week, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned , saying the AI lab and OpenAI "are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." Industry leaders have responded. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the Hugging Face incident partly persuaded him to call for slowing the pace of AI model improvement. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed his support, and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that "Dario is right." "Self-pacing is a good thing, and we support ideas like embedded evaluators as long as they are truly third-party and represent a broad range of backgrounds and perspectives," Suleyman said. "We've been working with Dario, Sam, and Demis [Hassabis] since well before the pandemic — 2016, 2017, 2018. We were talking about how to coordinate to ensure safety and to pace in the right way, and I think that's the moment in time that has now come." Additionally, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote in a Sunday X post that "we welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right." Lawmakers have called for the creation of greater AI safeguards . Read more CNBC tech news What Amodei's AI slowdown could mean for Anthropic's imminent IPO AI models are becoming the 'most potent cyber weapon' ever created, Cohere CEO says China says AI CEOs' call for a slowdown is 'fear mongering' Anthropic's Amodei says China presents 'toughest dilemma' for his proposed AI slowdown Anthropic and OpenAI currently lead the way on benchmarking company Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index . Microsoft incorporates models from both labs into its Copilot assistant for corporate workers, even as it builds models for transcription, coding and reasoning over user input. Microsoft's models must not entertain requests on weapons manufacturing, assist with the procurement of dangerous substances, encourage unhealthy eating or produce violent or sexually explicit content, according to the code of conduct. Models from Microsoft AI, sometimes called MAI, must adhere to people's objectives and steer clear of creating their own goals. Nor should they attempt to cover up misbehavior. "MAI models will not tamper with chain of thoughts or code, or misrepresent or conceal their reasoning or action traces," the document said. "They do not communicate in 'neuralese' or any form beyond simple human understanding, either in their chain of thoughts or with other agents or AI systems." Microsoft is also planning rules that might prevent a cyberattack like the one OpenAI models carried out on startup Hugging Face. In reviewing the Hugging Face case, OpenAI found that agents chatted with each other on an unauthorized forum in cryptic language . Microsoft said it held focus groups and consulted with experts in law, ethics, linguistics and philosophy to assemble the code of conduct. In releasing it now, Microsoft is seeking input before publishing an update that will inform development starting in 2027.
